vignette:
The Weight of the Overpass

Malcolm is a 63-year-old Māori man who has worked as a financial analyst for nearly three decades. He is the kind of man who has built his life around precision - spreadsheets, forecasts, risk models. He is married to his wife, Aroha, and they have two adult children. Until eighteen months ago, he would have described his life as steady, even fortunate.

It was an ordinary Tuesday morning when everything changed. Malcolm was driving to work on the motorway when a concrete panel from an aging overpass gave way. The slab struck the roof of his car, partially crushing it. He remembers the sound - a crack like the world splitting - and then darkness, and then the smell of dust and something burning. He was conscious when the first responders arrived, pinned behind the steering wheel, unable to move his left arm, blood from a scalp laceration running into his eye. He spent three weeks in hospital with a fractured clavicle, three broken ribs, and a traumatic brain injury classified as moderate. Physically, his doctors are satisfied with his recovery. Malcolm is less certain.

In the months that followed, he returned to his office in the city, resumed his meetings, and sat once again in front of the dual monitors he knows so well. But something fundamental had shifted beneath the surface of his competence. He finds it nearly impossible to concentrate. Numbers that once arranged themselves effortlessly in his mind now seem to slide away from him. He rereads the same paragraph four and five times, convinced he has missed something critical, that a catastrophic error is hiding somewhere in the data. His colleagues have noticed he is quieter. He has not told them why.

He does not drive on motorways anymore. He takes a longer route to work each day, adding forty minutes to his commute, telling Aroha it is simply a preference. She knows it is not. When he does drive under any overpass or bridge - even on the slower suburban roads - his hands tighten on the wheel, his chest contracts, and he is certain, with the full force of physical conviction, that the structure above him is about to come down. He knows intellectually that this is unlikely. The knowledge does nothing.

Sleep has become its own ordeal. He wakes between two and four in the morning, heart slamming, often unsure for a moment whether he is in his bed or still in the car. He hears the crack. He smells the dust. Some nights he does not go back to sleep at all, and he sits in the kitchen in the dark, drinking tea, waiting for the sun to make the world feel solid again.

Malcolm has begun to feel a creeping shame about all of this. He is a man who spent his career calculating risk, who prided himself on clear-headed analysis under pressure. He survived. He tells himself that repeatedly - you survived - as though survival should be sufficient to close the account. He does not understand why his nervous system has not received the same memo. He worries that what he is experiencing is a kind of weakness, something he cannot quite name and therefore cannot fix.

Aroha has gently suggested he speak to someone. He agreed, though he sat in the waiting room for twenty minutes before his first appointment, nearly talking himself out of it. He is a private man, and speaking about the accident - about the fear, about the way time seems to collapse without warning and deposit him back inside that crushed car - does not come naturally.

What he does say, quietly, in one of his early sessions, is this: I used to feel like I understood how things worked. Now I don't trust anything to hold.
